title: Three nights at Death's door
hookLine: three nights waiting at Death's door, and three wishes
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is as God
tomorrow: one wish left, and Death would rather not answer it

cards: A guest arrives, and nobody's home. He waits on the step. One night.
Two. Three. Nobody brings him so much as a glass of water.

The Katha takes that seriously: in a house where a brahmin guest waits without food, it says, the household's hopes, its good deeds, its children and its cattle are all put at risk. And this house belongs to Death.
Nachiketa is sitting on its step, three nights in, still hungry.

teach.b: Yama has been away. When he returns, his household tells him: a guest has been waiting, a young brahmin, like fire entering a house. Bring water.
Yama is appalled. This is a teaching Hindus still live by, atithi devo bhava, the guest is as God, and even Death keeps it. He bows to the boy: you stayed three nights in my house without eating.
For each night, choose a boon, a wish. Three wishes. Now watch what Nachiketa asks for.

teach.h: FIRST: LET MY FATHER BE AT PEACE.
teach.b: The first wish: let my father be calm again, no longer angry with me, and let him know me and welcome me when I'm sent back.
Of all the things to ask of Death, he asks first that the relationship with his father be healed. Yama grants it: your father will sleep peacefully, and his anger will be gone.

teach.h: SECOND: THE FIRE THAT LEADS TO HEAVEN.
teach.b: The second wish: teach me the fire ritual that leads to heaven, where there's no fear, no hunger, no old age.
Yama teaches it, and is so pleased with how quickly the boy learns that he names the fire after him: the Nachiketa fire. He even adds an extra gift, a chain or garland.
Two wishes, each one reasonable and generous, the kind a good son and a serious student would ask.
The third waits for tomorrow. But notice who Nachiketa is so far: a boy who waits, who forgives first, who learns fast. The two paths are about to open in front of him.

how: Hindu tradition treats the honoring of guests as sacred (atithi devo bhava, 'the guest is as God'); the Katha's opening is often told to show even Death keeping that duty.

games.q: a friend shows up at your door at dinnertime, unannounced. by the Katha, what fits?
o: send them home; you weren't expecting anyone.
water, a seat and a plate: the guest is as God.
let them wait outside until you've finished eating.
games.why: Yama was appalled a guest had waited three nights unfed, and gave a boon for each night. atithi devo bhava.

practice: Think of who might come through your door this week: family, a friend, a delivery driver, someone you didn't invite.

If you pray, ask that your home be a place where a guest is met the way God is met, the way Yama bowed to a hungry boy. If you don't, simply choose one small welcome to offer: water first, a seat, a plate.
And if someone is cross with you, borrow Nachiketa's first wish and wish them peace.

wordCard.voice: Vara, a boon, a chosen gift. Three nights at Death's door, then two boons: peace with his father, and the fire ritual that leads to heaven.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vara, a boon, a chosen gift; from vri, to choose. Yama offers three.

carryVoice: Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is as God. Even Death bowed to a hungry boy. Two hundred forty-seven days now.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1.10–1.1.19 (the first and second boons; the Nachiketa fire)
